summary.name: My week shadowing a GitLab Site Reliability Engineer
summary.one_liner: A 2019 GitLab blog post in which frontend engineer Tristan Read recounts a week shadowing an on-call Site Reliability Engineer, covering incidents, alert types, and the SRE tooling stack.
use_cases: Learning what a day-to-day on-call SRE role involves
Understanding how to classify monitoring alerts
Seeing a real example of handling a crypto-mining abuse incident on CI runners
Reviewing the tooling used by an SRE team (PagerDuty, Grafana, Kibana, Slack)
Ideas for improving incident response workflows inside an issue tracker
summary.what_it_does: The post is a first-person account by Tristan Read, a frontend engineer at GitLab, of shadowing an on-call SRE for one week in December 2019. It describes attending handover meetings, watching alert channels, and joining incident calls. It recounts two incidents: a spike in GitLab Runner usage caused by a user mining crypto, handled with an in-house abuse tool, and a slowdown with Apdex SLO violations on GitLab.com's canary and main web applications. It classifies alerts into fixed-threshold, percentage-based, and historical-average types, and argues the latter two are more useful for on-call work. It also lists internal and external tools used by the SRE team and suggests product improvements such as multi-user issue editing and more issue webhooks.
notable: First-person account of a week on call with a GitLab SRE, including a real crypto-mining abuse incident
Explains three alert types: fixed threshold, percentage of requests, and historical percentile
Lists the SRE toolchain: PagerDuty, Slack, Grafana, Kibana, Zoom Situation Room, GitLab issues and labels
caveats: Written in December 2019; tools and processes may have changed since
The crypto-mining incident issue is private and not visible to readers
